The boat hall is the heart of the museum and the place where most of a shift is spent. Visitors are
free to walk around all three boats and to climb the viewing platform beside the motor lifeboat, and
they may touch the hull of the inshore boat, which is there for that purpose. They may not board
any boat, lean on the pulling boat's oars, or lift children onto the platforms, and the volunteer on the
hall is expected to say so kindly and early rather than firmly and late.

The photographs along the north wall are copies and may be pointed at, photographed and, within
reason, touched. The originals are in the archive upstairs, which is not open to the public, and
requests to see them are passed to the archivist by email rather than promised on the spot. The
letters in the glass case are originals and the case is locked; the key is in the office and is not lent to
visitors under any circumstances, including descendants of the writers.

The audio guide is a set of handsets on the counter and it is free. It is also fragile, elderly and
unloved by its own manufacturer, so handsets are issued one per adult, signed out in the book, and
checked back in. A handset that does not come back is written up in the incident book the same day;
one that comes back broken goes in the box marked for repair with a note saying what happened,
and nobody attempts to mend it with tape, however tempting the roll on the bench looks.

Questions from visitors are the best part of the job and also the part most likely to go wrong.
Answer what you know, say plainly when you do not, and offer to find out; there is a card of the
commonest questions and their answers by the till. Do not guess at dates, names or the
circumstances of a rescue, because visitors frequently know more than they let on, and a confident
wrong answer travels further than a hesitant right one ever will, usually by way of the harbour cafe.

Dogs are welcome on a lead, pushchairs are welcome everywhere except the platform, and
wheelchair users can reach everything on the ground floor by the ramp at the side door, which a
volunteer opens on request. The lift to the archive is for staff and researchers only. If a visitor needs
it for access to the meeting room, a keyholder operates it and stays with the visitor for the whole of
the trip up and the whole of the trip down, without exception.

At the end of a hall shift, walk the room once more with the checklist, replace any handset left on a
bench, straighten the rope barriers, and note on the sheet anything that will need attention: a loose
board on the platform, a light out, a smell of damp in the corner by the slipway doors. Small things
written down get fixed on Thursday; small things remembered get forgotten by Friday and found
by a visitor on Saturday morning.
